prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We could hear her knocking down strands of cobweb from ceilings—sticky filaments, sacs of eggs—as we woke most mornings to a worm of discontent. It lodged beneath the heart, rubbed our frayed nerves, gnawed at the gut, spleen, ovaries. Filth was Mom's first enemy, so each day began with ritual cleaning: the stab and sweep of the broom down the dark hall, over the stained and scratched oak floors. For weeks, she held her dust mop one-handed, and with the other cupped a hernia, while she swore at us kids in that hard voice—a litany of our sins and failures: sloth, stupidity, secrecy. We watched her smash the spiders that ran, herky-jerky, along the baseboards, while we ran, too. Glaring at each other, we gathered up the scattered laundry, our father’s shoes, his newspapers and tools, our books, drawings, music, sweatshirts, and jackets, whatever we’d left lying around. We were guilty, but good at evasion. We cultivated shrewish or obsessive behaviors of our own: my tough older sister sneered and stalked out of the house to meet her boyfriend; my sweet younger sister trembled and cried, comforted by one of our many dogs. I slammed doors, pounded them with my fists, screamed, “Shut up, shut up, shut up!” She couldn’t leave us alone. She loved us too much. Though we were quick, she was quicker. Her words stung. We must have deserved it.

Most days began with a deep-seated dread settling inside us—a raw anxiety affecting our chests, nerves, and lower abdomens—as the sound of our mother clearing sticky webs and egg clusters from the high corners filled the house. Dirt was her ultimate adversary, making a morning cleaning ritual mandatory. We would hear the sharp thud and scrape of her broom moving down the unlit hallway across worn, marked hardwood. For several weeks, she steered her dust mop using a single hand while pressing the other against a painful hernia, all the while harshly berating us. Her stern voice rattled off our various flaws, condemning us for being lazy, foolish, and deceptive. 

As she stomped on the erratic spiders scurrying near the floorboards, we scrambled away as well. Exchanging frustrated looks, we hurried to pick up the clutter left behind: our father's footwear, reading material, and equipment, alongside our own literature, artwork, sheet music, hoodies, coats, and stray laundry. We recognized our own culpability, yet we were skilled at dodging her wrath. 

In response, we each formed our own obsessive or abrasive coping mechanisms. My hardened elder sister would scoff and storm out of the house to see her partner, whereas my gentle little sister would shake and weep, finding comfort beside one of our many dogs. My own reaction was violent: I battered and slammed doors, screaming at her to be quiet. Still, she was incapable of giving us space, driven by an intense love. Rapid as we were, she was always faster, and her sharp comments caused real pain. In the end, we likely brought her treatment upon ourselves.

Every morning began not with the gentle rise of the sun, but with the violent symphony of domestic warfare. Before the rest of the household could even stretch awake, the mother initiated her ritualistic cleaning routine. Driven by an obsessive need to purge the house of any trace of dirt or imaginary pests, she attacked the floors with harsh chemicals and aggressive strokes of the broom, transforming the sanctuary of home into an unrelenting battleground. 

This relentless crusade continued unabated, even when she was in visible physical agony. Suffering from a painful hernia that made every movement an ordeal, her bodily distress seemed only to sharpen her tongue. Refusing to rest, she directed her torment outward, relentlessly berating her children with a barrage of sharp insults. With every scrub of the counter, she pelted them with accusations of failure and inadequacy, using her pain as fuel for her cruel verbal assaults.

Terrified of attracting her unpredictable wrath, the children lived in a state of hyper-vigilance. The sound of a clattering bucket or a heavy sigh was their cue to scramble. In a desperate bid for self-preservation, they moved swiftly through the hallways, rapidly gathering their scattered clothes, books, and toys. They attempted to erase all physical proof of their presence from the living spaces, hoping that an immaculate home might buy them a few moments of peace.

Yet, no amount of tidy countertops could truly shield their spirits, forcing each sibling to construct their own psychological defenses to survive the tense environment. The house became a study in distinct human coping mechanisms. One sibling chose defiance, hardening their heart and meeting the mother's vitriol with quiet rebellion. Another absorbed the hurt inward, collapsing into silent tears at the first raised voice. A third sibling mirrored the home's volatile atmosphere, responding to the stress with explosive outbursts of their own anger.

Through it all, the narrator occupied a painfully complex emotional middle ground. Though the mother’s stinging words cut deeply—leaving psychological scars that lingered long after the shouting stopped—the narrator developed a paradoxical perspective. To survive the distress, the narrator reframed the abuse, convincing themselves that this harsh, suffocating behavior was not born of malice, but was instead a fierce, albeit deeply warped, expression of maternal love.

The house did not smell of bread or woodsmoke; it smelled of raw bleach, pine oil, and hot iron. Long before the sun cleared the horizon, the silence of the morning was shattered by the harsh, rhythmic rasp of a scrub brush against linoleum. 

Margaret moved through the rooms like a tortured general waging a war she knew she was destined to lose. Her body was a map of physical suffering—a bad hip that clicked with every step, swollen, arthritic knuckles, and a lower back calcified by decades of hard labor. Yet, her pain was no match for her terror of filth. To Margaret, dirt was not merely unhygienic; it was a physical manifestation of sin, a moral rot creeping under the doorframes to corrupt her family. Dust was laziness, a stain was a secret vice, and unorganized clutter was evidence of a soul in disarray.

Every day was a crusade. Hobbling on her good leg, she dragged the heavy vacuum across the carpets, wiped down walls that were already spotless, and sanitized door handles until the brass wore thin. And throughout it all, her voice was the constant backdrop to her children’s lives—a sharp, shrill sermon of condemnation. 

"Look at this!" she would shriek, pointing a bent, trembling finger at a lone pair of socks left beside a chair. "I ruin my hands for you! I tear my back to pieces keeping this house holy, and you wallow in your own garbage like animals! You have no respect for this home, no respect for God, and no respect for me!"

Her four children learned to navigate the domestic minefield, each developing a distinct emotional armor to survive the daily onslaught. 

Leo, the oldest, chose defiance. He met her berating with a stony, callous silence, deliberately leaving his boots on by the door just to watch her fume. His rebellion was a wall he built to keep her from breaking his spirit, though it earned him the brunt of her wrath. 

Maya, the middle daughter, crumbled into a state of perpetual panic. She spent her afternoons trailing behind her mother with a dustpan, her cheeks wet with tears, desperately trying to preempt the outbursts. She washed her own hands until they were raw and bleeding, apologizing for mistakes she hadn’t even made. 

Julian, the youngest, absorbed the tension like a sponge until he couldn't hold it anymore. His coping mechanism was sudden, terrifying rage. A sharp word from Margaret over an unmade bed would trigger an explosion—a slammed door, a shattered glass, a screamed curse—followed by hours of hiding in the dark of his closet, trembling with shame.

Yet, the cruelest paradox of the household was that Margaret did not act out of malice. Her terror of dust was wrapped tightly around a suffocating, desperate love. She washed their clothes until the fabric frayed because she believed a clean child was a safe child. She stayed up until midnight ironing their shirts while her hip throbbed with agony, weeping quietly over the ironing board because she wanted them to be "respectable" in a world she viewed as cruel and unforgiving. She burned herself out on the altar of her devotion, and she made sure her children felt the heat of the fire.

As the years wore on, the children grew up and scattered, leaving the scrubbed-clean house behind. But the chlorine scent of Margaret’s obsession followed them into adulthood. 

Though they had hated the rituals and resented the endless sermons, the damage was done. They carried the lingering stain of her overbearing love beneath their skins. In their own homes, a stray crumb on the counter or a stack of unread mail would trigger an unexplainable wave of dread. They had inherited her agony without ever meaning to, bound forever by a profound, agonizing guilt—the belief that no matter how hard they scrubbed, they would never be quite clean enough to deserve her sacrifice.
outputs.L5:
To the rest of the world, it was just filth. It was the stubborn grease etched into the deep lines of her palms, the crescent moons of dark soot beneath her fingernails, and the faint, lingering scent of industrial soap that no sweet-smelling perfume could ever fully mask. 

Mom wore that grime like a second skin. 

When I was a child, I didn’t understand it. There were times I felt a quiet, childish shame when she arrived at school events straight from her shift, her heavy work boots caked in mud and her canvas jacket stained with the day's hard labor. I envied the other children whose mothers smelled like vanilla and wore immaculate, cream-colored sweaters. I mistook her messy appearance for neglect, unable to see the profound beauty hidden beneath the grime.

It took growing up—and facing the harsh realities of the world myself—for me to finally understand. 

Her dirty hands were the exact reason mine were clean. 

Every hour Mom spent wading through the literal and metaphorical filth of the world was a deliberate sacrifice. She scrubbed down the greasy machinery of factories, hauled heavy earth, and cleared away the debris of difficult jobs, taking on the dirt so that it would never touch me. She bore the heat, the sweat, and the stains day after day, driven by an unwavering sense of duty. 

It was all for me. 

It was for my school books, my clean clothes, the warmth of a bright kitchen, and the chance to choose a life of my own. She willingly immersed herself in the grit of survival so that I could reach for something higher. 

Now, when I look at my mom’s aging hands resting quietly in her lap, I don't see dirt at all. I see honor. I see an unbroken history of love written in calluses and worn skin. She endured the filth of the world so that I could walk through it unblemished, and for that, I will spend the rest of my life holding those beautiful hands with nothing less than pride.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary scene from a memoir about growing up with an obsessively clean, angry mother. Show how the narrator and their siblings had different ways of coping with her daily morning rituals.
counterfactuals.output:
At 6:15 a.m., our house did not wake to birdsong or the gentle warmth of the sun; it woke to the citrus-and-bleach aerosolized hostility of my mother’s morning purge. 

Before the tea kettle even whistled, the house was already vibrating. First came the violent, rhythmic *thump-slap* of the Hoover vacuum biting into the baseboards, driven by an arm that moved not with the rhythm of domestic care, but with the frantic energy of an exorcism. Next was the sharp, misting hiss of Windex, followed by the squeak of paper towels rubbed raw against glass. My mother cleaned the way other people waged war: relentlessly, loudly, and with a burning, unassailable sense of righteousness. To her, a stray crumb wasn’t just dirt; it was a personal betrayal, a sign that her children were actively conspiring to rot her life from the inside out.

We were three animals responding to the same predator, each of us having evolved a distinct survival strategy by the time we reached middle school.

My older brother, Julian, chose armor. When her angry footsteps stomped up the stairs, he would simply pull the heavy down comforter over his head and transform himself into stone. Even when she tore the covers off him, screaming that he was lazy, filthy, and pig-headed, Julian would lie there on his back, eyes fixed on the ceiling, completely blank. He had learned the art of psychological absence. She could yell at his meat and bones, but Julian himself had backed out of the room, out of the house, out of the universe. His silence infuriated her more than open rebellion, but it kept his heart intact.

My younger sister, Clara, was the appease-and-assimilate type. The moment the vacuum clicked on, she would bolt out of bed, her face pale, her hands trembling. By 6:20, she was already down in the kitchen, clutching a damp microfiber cloth like a sacrificial offering. "I can wipe the lower cabinets, Mommy," she’d plead, her voice small and tight with terror. Clara believed that if she became an extension of the rage, the rage wouldn't turn on her. She scrubbed until her fingers were raw and pruned with pine oil, desperate to buy a few minutes of conditional love with a streak-free surface.

I was the ghost. 

My strategy was total physical erasure. I moved through the hallway without letting the floorboards creak. I had perfected a method of making my bed while still half-in it, smoothing the flat sheet into tight, military-grade hospital corners before my feet even touched the rug. I didn't use the bathroom until she moved to the kitchen; I didn't breathe too loudly when she passed my door. If I left no footprint, no shadow, and no dust, I could not be accused of defiling her shrine. I became so adept at becoming invisible that sometimes I wondered if I was actually there at all.

By 7:00 a.m., the kitchen smelled so fiercely of ammonia it made our eyes water over our dry cereal. My mother stood over the island, her knuckles white against the granite, her breathing shallow, scanning the gleaming surfaces for a flaw we hadn't yet committed. 

Clara hovered at her elbow, waiting for approval that would never come. Julian stared straight ahead into his bowl, wrapped in his invisible suit of armor. And I sat quietly in the corner, eating my cornflakes with calculated, silent precision, careful not to let the spoon click against the porcelain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a story excerpt about a dysfunctional family where a mother's obsession with cleanliness manifests as physical and verbal intensity toward her kids? Make it poetic and slightly dark.
counterfactuals.output:
In our house, salvation smelled of sodium hypochlorite and artificial lemon. It was a holy sting that burned the back of the throat, an incense that declared the devil of dirt had been temporarily banished. 

Mother did not walk through the rooms; she patrolled them. She was a high-priestess of the pristine, her hands perpetually cracked and blooming with raw, red knuckles—not from cold, but from the relentless, caustic love she poured into the porcelain. 

My brother, Leo, committed the evening’s transgression. He was seven, built of soft edges and careless movements, and he had dared to bring a smudge of garden soil into the hallway on the welt of his shoe. 

The air in the house shifted instantly. The silence became heavy, pressurized, like the atmosphere before a strike of lightning. 

Mother’s eyes locked onto the black streak. They were not the eyes of a parent, but of a mortal threatened by a quiet contagion. She moved without sound, her yellow rubber gloves glistening under the harsh wattage of the overhead bulb. 

"Look at what you’ve done," she whispered. Her voice was terrifyingly soft, a razor drawn slowly across wet glass. "You drag the rot inside. You bring the filth to my table."

Leo froze, a rabbit caught in the glare of a cruel sun. "I forgot to take off my—"

"Quiet!" The word snapped through the hall, a whip-crack of pure, unadulterated venom. 

She seized his wrist. Her grip was not a mother’s guidance, but a clamp of cold steel. She dragged him down to his knees before the smudge, her breathing coming in thin, wet rattles. From her apron pocket, she produced the brass-bristled brush—the heavy one reserved for the grout, for the deep sins. 

"You think you can ruin this?" She pressed his small face down, not quite touching the floor, but close enough for him to smell the dry dust of his own making. "I scrub and I scrub until my bones ache, and you walk in here like a animal. A filthy, shameless little animal."

She didn't scrub the floor first. She scrubbed his hands. 

She turned the tap in the hallway sink until the water ran scalding, filling the small space with a thick, suffocating steam. She caught Leo’s fingers and hauled them under the torrent, applying the bar of harsh carbolic soap until the foam ran thick and gray. 

"Clean," she chanted, a dark litany whispered into the crown of his hair as he whimpered, his small body trembling violently against her knees. She squeezed his forearm until her fingertips left white moons in his flesh. "I will make you clean, Leo. Even if I have to strip the skin from your bones to find the good inside you."

*Scritch. Scritch.* The rough sponge scraped against his tender knuckles. Leo didn't cry out loud—we had learned early that tears were liquid, liquid left spots, and spots required another round of bleach. He only swallowed his sobs, his eyes wide and glassy, fixing on mine where I stood frozen in the dark of the doorway.

I pressed my back against the wall, holding my breath, shrinking into the shadows. In Mother’s house, to be seen was to be dirty. And to be dirty was to be destroyed, rendered down by hot water and furious hands until there was nothing left of us at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vignette focusing on a childhood memory of a home dominated by an overbearing parent. Include sensory details like broom sweeps, spider hunting, and the distinct reactions of three siblings.
counterfactuals.output:
At four o’clock every afternoon, the house ceased to belong to us and became the domain of the broom. 

It was a heavy thing made of coarse, unbleached straw that rattled like dry bone against the baseboards. *Rasp-drag, thump. Rasp-drag, thump.* Mother moved through the hallway with a terrifying, metronomic efficiency, her spine a rod of cold iron, her feet bare against the dark heart-pine floorboards. The air always smelled of her two obsessions: lemon wax and crushed clove cigarettes.

"Insects," she would mutter to the empty corridor, her voice low and sharp as a clipped fingernail. "Neglect breeds rot. Rot brings the creeping things."

She halted mid-sweep in the archway of the sitting room, the straw bristles flexed and straining against the wood. Her gaze locked onto the high corner above the door frame. 

There, suspended in a triangle of pale sunlight, hung a small spider—a yellow garden orb weaver, no larger than a rain drop, hanging from a line of spun glass.

"Look at it," Mother commanded. She didn't raise her voice, but the draft in the room seemed to freeze. "Look how quickly the wild takes over when you turn your back."

We were positioned like statues around the room, each of us frozen in our well-rehearsed survival postures.

Julian, fourteen and bursting at the seams of his clothes, stood beside the sideboard. His reaction was a silent, simmering rage. His jaw was clenched so hard the muscles jumped beneath his skin, his fists stuffed deep into his pockets, bunching the denim. He stared directly at the back of Mother’s head, his dark eyes wide and unblinking—a furious, impotent defiance that begged her to turn around and catch him glaring.

On the bottom step of the staircase, seven-year-old Clara sought invisibility. At the sound of Mother’s voice, she had pulled her knees up to her chest and dragged her oversized wool sweater down over her shins, tucking her head into the collar like a turtle retreating into a shell. She was picking violently at a loose thread on her hem, her breathing so shallow it barely moved the knit fabric. If she didn't breathe, if she didn't move, the broom wouldn't find her.

I sat at the mahogany table, six inches from the edge, my arithmetic workbook open before me. My reaction was hyper-vigilance. I didn't look at Julian, and I didn't look at Clara. I tracked Mother’s weight as she shifted from her left heel to her right ball. I calculated the arc of the broom. I knew that if the straw struck the wall at a forty-five-degree angle, dust would scatter toward my papers, and a smudge on my margin meant an extra hour of copying the dictionary.

Mother reversed her grip on the long wooden handle. She raised the broom head-first toward the ceiling, the dried straw whispering against the wallpaper.

The spider twitched, sensing the shift in air pressure. 

*Thud.*

The impact vibrated through the plaster, shaking a fine haze of white dust into the ambient sunlight. Mother dragged the stiff head of the broom down the wall with a sickening *shhhk*, smearing a pale grey streak across the cream paint. The tiny body of the spider vanished into the yellow fibers.

"Clean," Mother declared, lowering the broom with a heavy sigh that smelled of clove. She didn't look at any of us, but her presence pressed against our chests, suffocating and vast. 

She turned and resumed her cadence—*rasp-drag, thump, rasp-drag, thump*—heading down the hall toward the kitchen. 

Only when the sound of the straw moved into the back of the house did the room exhale. Julian let out a shaky, jagged breath and slammed his hand against his thigh. Clara slowly peeked out from her wool collar, her eyes wide and wet. And I carefully, silently, blew the tiny speck of plaster dust off the corner of my page before it could leave a mark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output: Every dinner was a silent tightrope walk I carefully engineered, watching Leo’s knuckles turn white against his fork while Maya held her breath, terrified that the wrong pitch of her laugh might shatter the fragile peace. I knew precisely which subtle sigh would make my son apologize for a mistake he hadn't made, and exactly how long to withhold my warmth from my daughter until she fractured, desperate to rebuild herself in whatever shape I demanded. They flinched at my sharpness, looking at me with those wounded, betraying eyes whenever I picked apart their small triumphs—pointing out the microscopic flaws in Maya’s perfect report card or the fatal softness in Leo’s demeanor—never understanding that a wild, untended child is easily destroyed by the cruel frost of the real world. It was exhausting, carrying the heavy, solitary burden of their quiet resentment, but as I watched them tremble beneath my gaze, perfectly obedient and shielded from their own weakness, I swallowed the ache in my chest and remembered that true devotion isn't sweet; it is the butcher's blade that cuts away the decay, and no one else would ever love them enough to break them so beautifully.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose passage about a mother who cleans the house relentlessly every morning while berating her children.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the sun had even cleared the line of pines behind the backyard, the house belonged to the bleach. 

The morning did not begin with the soft light of dawn or the gentle chatter of birds; it began with the violent, rhythmic *thunk-thunk-thunk* of the vacuum baseboard-bashing its way down the hallway. It was 5:45 AM, and Martha was already at war.

She moved through the rooms like a natural disaster in a faded floral bathrobe, her rubber gloves squeaking with furious friction. To Martha, a speck of dust was not an inevitability of living; it was a personal insult, a treasonous conspiracy orchestrated by the three human beings she had brought into the world.

"Get up! Look at this! Just look at it!" Her voice scraped through the floorboards, cutting through the thin blanket of her eldest son’s sleep. She slammed his bedroom door open with enough force to rattle the glass in the windowpane. "Absolute swine! I live with absolute swine!"

She ripped the covers off twelve-year-old Leo, leaving him shivering in his pajamas. She wasn't looking at him; her eyes were locked onto a stray sock curled near the base of his desk. 

"I slave away," she hissed, swooping down to snap the sock off the carpet as if it were a venomous snake. "Six o'clock in the morning, and I am on my knees while the lot of you sleep like royalty. Ungrateful, lazy little parasites. You think a maid lives here? You think money grows on the weeds you drag into my carpet?"

In the adjacent room, eight-year-old Maya sat bolt upright in bed, her tiny feet pulled tightly against her chest, waiting for the hurricane to shift direction. It always did. 

Martha pushed the vacuum with the force of a battering ram, gouging the baseboards, using the roar of the motor as a backing track to her vitriol. She swept through the living room, tearing cushions off the sofa to vacuum the dark, hidden seams, cursing the microscopic crumbs she found there. 

"I ruined my back for you!" she shouted over the whine of the motor, spraying Lemon Pledge into the air with the frantic cadence of a soldier firing blind into the fog. "I haven't had a moment of peace since 2012! Not a single person in this house respects me. Not one!"

She threw open the windows, letting the freezing morning air rush in to chase away the smell of sleep, indifferent to her children who huddled in the hallway, clutching their elbows, terrified to step on the damp, freshly mopped linoleum. 

By seven, the house was sterile. The air smelled blindingly of ammonia and pine, so sharp it burned the back of the throat. The hardwood floors gleamed like ice, mirror-shined and treacherous. 

In the kitchen, Martha stood over the stove, pouring boiling water into a mug. Her bathrobe was damp at the cuffs, her hair escaping its tight bun in damp, furious wisps. She looked at her children, who sat at the kitchen island, frozen, barely daring to breathe, let alone reach for the box of cereal. 

"Well?" Martha snapped, her voice raspy from shouting, her eyes hollow with the exhaustion of her own making. "What are you staring at? Eat your breakfast. And if a single crumb hits that floor, so help me God."
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
